segments.vo: A wave of molasses once killed twenty-one people. This really happened.
January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen. Boston's North End.
Right by the harbor stood a giant steel tank.
Fifty feet tall, towering over the street.
segments.cap: 50 feet tall, towering over the street.

segments.vo: Inside, two point three million gallons of molasses.
It was going to be turned into industrial alcohol.
It leaked so badly that local kids filled pails with the drips.
The fix? Paint the tank brown, so the leaks wouldn't show.
Then, in the middle of winter, the temperature jumped above forty degrees.
segments.cap: Then, in the middle of winter, the temperature jumped above 40°F.

segments.vo: And early that afternoon, the tank burst apart.
A wave of molasses raced through the streets at thirty-five miles an hour.
segments.cap: A wave of molasses raced through the streets at 35 mph.

segments.vo: It flattened buildings and knocked a train off the elevated railway.
Twenty-one people died. About one hundred fifty were injured.
Boston Harbor stayed brown until summer.
One hundred nineteen people sued, and the tank's owner was found responsible.
segments.cap: 119 people sued, and the tank's owner was found responsible.

segments.vo: It paid six hundred twenty-eight thousand dollars.
And the disaster changed the law: engineers had to sign and seal their plans.
For decades, locals said the area still smelled of molasses on hot days.
